Notes: Earliest documented Judean presence at Susa (basis of Year Established): promissory note OECT 10 152 (= Bloch 2014 text no. 7), dated 18-I-28 Darius I = 494 BCE, from the Egibi family archive of Babylon, recording the presence of prominent Babylonians in the Persian capital Susa. Among the parties and witnesses is Yahu-shar-usur son of Shamash-iddin, whose name carries the Yahwistic element; Alstola takes him as a Judean connected to the royal administration in Babylonia who came to Susa on tax business (Persian kings made Babylonian officials and businessmen visit the court regularly), so he was a visitor rather than a proven resident. Alstola (pp. 36-37) also states that Judean presence in Susa in the early 5th c. BCE is confirmed by cuneiform sources; Bloch 2014 discusses these men as Judeans at the Susa court. Scale: individual Judean officials, no community figure. Not counted as earlier documented presence: Esther 2:6 (Mordecai exiled with Jeconiah, 597 BCE) and Daniel 8:2 (vision 'in Shushan', 3rd year of Belshazzar), both treated by Alstola as literary fiction; the Talmudic tradition listing Shush among places of exile of the ten tribes and the medieval tradition of Daniel's tomb at Susa are tradition, not documented presence.

Promissory note VS 6 155 (= Bloch 2014 text no. 8), dated 6-VIII-29 Darius I = 493 BCE, from the Ilia archive of Borsippa, also recording Babylonians present at Susa. It names Shabbataya son of Nabu-shar-bullit (a West Semitic name often borne by Judeans) and Nabu-ahhe-shullim son of Aqbi-il (West Semitic patronymic). Alstola: Shabbataya's Judean origin 'remains no more than a possibility'; he was probably a Babylonian official in Susa on tax-related matters (visitor). Possible single Judean individual; Population blank.

Book of Esther (literary attestation): the source identifies Ahasuerus with Xerxes I (486-465 BCE); Esther is married to the king in his seventh year (c. 479 BCE); the story is set in Susa, and Esther asks that 'the Jews in Susa fast' for three days - in the narrative an organized Jewish community in Susa. No number of Jews given. Historicity is disputed: this source defends it, while many scholars (e.g. Alstola, Macchi) regard the book as largely fictional diaspora literature.

Esther 9:6-18 (also 4:16; KJV): c. 473 BCE (Adar following the 12th year of Ahasuerus, Esther 3:7; date assumes Ahasuerus = Xerxes I). 'The Jews that were in Shushan' gathered on 13 and 14 Adar; they slew 500 men in Shushan the palace (9:6, 9:12) plus Haman's ten sons, and 300 more men in Shushan on 14 Adar (9:15); 75,000 were slain in the other provinces (9:16). These are casualty counts of their enemies, not the Jewish population, so Population is blank. Esther 4:16 'gather together all the Jews that are present in Shushan' implies a Jewish community in the city in the narrative. Literary text of disputed historicity.

Nehemiah 1:1-4 and 2:1 (KJV): Nehemiah son of Hachaliah, a Judean serving as the king's cupbearer, was 'in Shushan the palace' in the month Kislev of the twentieth year (of Artaxerxes, Neh 2:1; Artaxerxes I, so c. 445 BCE). There Hanani 'one of my brethren' and 'certain men of Judah' came to him from Judah (visitors). Documents a Judean courtier at the Persian court in Susa; no community size given. No evidence for Jews at Susa (Seleucia on the Eulaeus) in the Hellenistic or Parthian periods (to 74 CE) was found in the sources searched.
